On the Alzer–Berg problem: an optimal Bernstein boundary and a uniqueness conjecture

Valmir Krasniqi Address: Institute of Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics (STEM), Rr. Nekibe Kelmendi Nr. 26, 10000 Prishtinë, Republic of Kosovo Email address: valmir@stem-ks.org
Abstract.

We study the two-parameter exponential family associated with the complete-monotonicity problem of Alzer and Berg. Strict necessary parameter bounds place every possible Bernstein function in the domain of a regularized Laplace representation. A quantitative positivity-transfer inequality then yields a linear sufficient condition with the largest possible universal coefficient, expressed in terms of the exact one-parameter critical exponent. To describe the whole admissible region, we derive convolution identities for parameter derivatives and prove that increasing either normalized parameter destroys positivity at every zero of a nonnegative density. Combined with uniform tail estimates, this excludes gaps in the admissible parameter intervals and gives a continuous, strictly monotone optimal boundary. Global nonnegativity of the density and contact with zero characterize that boundary; its inverse determines the complete admissible interval for the second parameter. The characterization is implicit and requires neither uniqueness nor nondegeneracy of the contact points. Published numerical approximations of the one-parameter exponent are distinguished from the exact results and from the finite rational certificate used in the proofs. We also derive a variational formula and a rigorous framework for validated numerical enclosure of the boundary, and formulate a boundary-contact conjecture asserting uniqueness and quadratic contact at every interior boundary point.

Key words and phrases: 
Bernstein function, complete monotonicity, Laplace density, positivity transfer, optimal boundary, convolution identity
2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
Primary 26A48, 44A10; Secondary 30E20

1. Introduction

1.1. Historical background and the Alzer–Berg problem

Complete monotonicity relates alternating derivative inequalities to positive integral representations. Its classical foundations include Bernstein’s work on absolutely monotone functions [8] and Widder’s treatment of Laplace transforms [12]. The corresponding class of Bernstein functions is central to potential theory and the theory of convolution semigroups; systematic accounts are given by Berg and Forst [5], Berg [4], and Schilling, Song and Vondraček [10]. These connections make parameter-dependent elementary functions useful test cases: an elementary formula may conceal a delicate global positivity problem for its representing measure.

We consider

(1.1) Fa,b​(x)=(1+ax)x+b,a>0,b∈ℝ,x>0,F_{a,b}(x)=\left(1+\dfrac{a}{x}\right)^{x+b},\qquad a>0,\quad b\in\mathbb{R},\quad x>0,

and write Pa,b​(x)=ea−Fa,b​(x)P_{a,b}(x)=e^{a}-F_{a,b}(x). In 2002, Alzer and Berg [1, p. 458] asked for all pairs (a,b)(a,b) for which Pa,bP_{a,b} is completely monotone. They established the case b=0b=0, 0<a≤10<a\leq 1. The same paper characterizes complete monotonicity of the opposite difference Fa,b−eaF_{a,b}-e^{a} by the condition a≤2​ba\leq 2b [1, Theorem 4]. That result concerns a different sign and a different parameter region; it does not answer the question for Pa,bP_{a,b}. Their subsequent paper [2] develops further classes of completely monotone functions and provides additional context for this line of investigation.

1.2. The one-parameter problem and later developments

Berg [3] reformulated the slice b=0b=0 in terms of the Bernstein property of

(1.2) hα​(y)=(1+1y)α​y,α>0,y>0.h_{\alpha}(y)=\left(1+\dfrac{1}{y}\right)^{\alpha y},\qquad\alpha>0,\quad y>0.

The scaling Fa,0​(a​y)=ha​(y)F_{a,0}(ay)=h_{a}(y) identifies the two formulations. Closure under positive powers of order at most one and under pointwise limits shows that the admissible exponents form an initial interval with an included endpoint; see also [6, Section 1]. The problem therefore leads to an exact critical exponent α∗\alpha_{*}, rather than to a separate test for every derivative order.

Shemyakova, Khashin and Jeffrey [11] investigated the one-parameter problem computationally through high-order derivatives and obtained numerical evidence for a critical value near 2.2996564432.299656443. Berg, Massa and Peron [6] subsequently constructed entire Laplace densities for eα−hαe^{\alpha}-h_{\alpha} and derived coefficient expansions in terms of Bell polynomials. Their work connects these densities with the Bessel function J1J_{1} and the Lambert WW function, and reports the more precise approximation

(1.3) α∗≈2.29965644325346130332.\alpha_{*}\approx 2.29965644325346130332.

The decimal in (1.3) is taken from the part of [6, Theorem 1.7] explicitly designated as numerical results. Here it is used only for illustration, not as an exact value or a certified enclosure.

Related work addresses stronger or complementary properties of the same one-parameter family. Berg and Pedersen [7] identify those members whose derivatives are logarithmically completely monotone, leading to the class of Horn–Bernstein functions. Cao, Guo, Du and Qi [9] derive formulas for higher derivatives using partial Bell polynomials and give a one-parameter threshold characterization. These results concern the slice (1.2); they do not supply the coordinatewise ordering and the two-parameter boundary established below. In particular, the existence of the one-parameter threshold and its published numerical approximation are not claimed as new results of this paper.

1.3. Main results and scope

Recall that g∈C∞​(0,∞)g\in C^{\infty}(0,\infty) is completely monotone if (−1)n​g(n)≥0(-1)^{n}g^{(n)}\geq 0 for every integer n≥0n\geq 0. A nonnegative smooth function ff is a Bernstein function if f′f^{\prime} is completely monotone. We write CM\mathrm{CM} and BF\mathrm{BF} for these classes. The Bernstein representation is

(1.4) f⁡(x)=k+𝑑x+∫(0,∞)(1−e−x​t)​μ​(𝑑t),f(x)=k+dx+\int_{(0,\infty)}(1-e^{-xt})\,\mu(\mathrm{d}t),

where k,d≥0k,d\geq 0 and ∫(0,∞)min⁡{1,t}​μ​(𝑑t)<∞\int_{(0,\infty)}\min\{1,t\}\,\mu(\mathrm{d}t)<\infty; see [10, Theorem 3.2]. Scaling the argument by a positive number preserves the Bernstein property. Since Fa,b​(x)→eaF_{a,b}(x)\to e^{a} as x→∞x\to\infty, we have

(1.5) Fa,b∈BF⟺Pa,b∈CM.F_{a,b}\in\mathrm{BF}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad P_{a,b}\in\mathrm{CM}.

Indeed, the derivative signs coincide, and a Bernstein Fa,bF_{a,b} is increasing and bounded above by its limit. This is a special instance of the relation between bounded Bernstein functions and completely monotone complements; compare [4, Remark 5.5].

The present paper separates three questions that must not be conflated. Necessary inequalities restrict where the Bernstein property can hold. An explicit sufficient region gives parameter pairs for which it does hold. An exact boundary description must additionally account for every admissible pair, exclude gaps, and establish the behavior of the boundary as a parameter varies. A sufficient line with the best universal coefficient need not coincide with that boundary at any fixed negative value of bb.

Our first contribution is a regularized, integrable Laplace density whose domain covers every possible Bernstein pair. The coverage follows from necessary inequalities proved independently of the positivity arguments. A quantitative comparison between normalized densities then gives the sufficient condition a≤α∗​(1+b)a\leq\alpha_{*}(1+b) for −1<b≤0-1<b\leq 0. The coefficient α∗\alpha_{*} is optimal among constants valid for all such bb, although the true admissible interval is strictly larger for each fixed −1<b<0-1<b<0.

The second contribution is a density-level argument for coordinatewise ordering of the full admissible set. Convolution identities show that, at every zero of a nonnegative density, increasing either normalized parameter makes the density negative. Uniform tail estimates turn this local fact into a global no-gap theorem. Consequently, the whole Bernstein region is described by 0<a≤A⁡(b)0<a\leq A(b), where AA is continuous and strictly increasing on (−1,0](-1,0]. The inverse boundary gives the complete admissible interval for bb when aa is fixed.

The resulting description is exact but implicit. At the boundary the density is globally nonnegative and touches zero at a positive argument. The global inequality is essential: solving the two tangency equations alone does not certify admissibility. We neither assume nor prove uniqueness of the contact point, multiplicity exactly two, or differentiability of the boundary. A variational formula and a rigorous framework for validated numerical enclosure are developed later. Motivated by the contact equations and the local continuation theorem, we finally formulate the conjecture that every interior boundary density has exactly one positive zero and that this zero has multiplicity two.

1.4. Organization and notation

We use CM\mathrm{CM} and BF\mathrm{BF} for the classes of completely monotone and Bernstein functions, respectively. Throughout the normalized formulation we write c=−bc=-b, so that 0≤c<10\leq c<1 corresponds to −1<b≤0-1<b\leq 0. The symbol α∗\alpha_{*} denotes the exact one-parameter critical exponent defined in Section 4; decimal values quoted for it are used only for numerical orientation.

The auxiliary results precede the main theorems. Section 2 proves the necessary restrictions, and Section 3 constructs the density and its uniform tail estimates. Section 4 treats the exact one-parameter exponent and proves the positivity-transfer inequality. The sharp linear sufficient theorem appears in Section 5. Section 6 establishes the parameter-convolution identities and excludes gaps. Section 7 proves the optimal-boundary theorem, develops the variational and continuation formulations, and gives the inverse description. Section 8 compares the bounds and records illustrative examples. The paper closes in Section 9 with a boundary-contact uniqueness conjecture and several concrete open problems suggested by the theory.

3. The regularized Laplace density

3.1. Normalization and the Bernstein criterion

It is convenient to replace bb by c=−bc=-b and work with

(3.1) Ha,c​(y)=(1+1y)a​y−c,a>0,0≤c<1.H_{a,c}(y)=\left(1+\dfrac{1}{y}\right)^{ay-c},\qquad a>0,\quad 0\leq c<1.

Then

(3.2) Fa,b​(a​y)=Ha,−b​(y).F_{a,b}(ay)=H_{a,-b}(y).

Remark 4 (Coverage of all possible Bernstein parameters).

By Proposition 2 and (3.2), Ha,c∈BFH_{a,c}\in\mathrm{BF} entails a+c<K0<3a+c<K_{0}<3. Thus the hypothesis a+c<3a+c<3 in Proposition 3 excludes no possible Bernstein function in this family. Conversely, a+c<3a+c<3 alone guarantees only a signed Laplace representation, not positivity of its density.

Remark 7.

The exact localization (4.2) is sufficient for the transfer argument. The published decimal (1.3) is used only to illustrate the size of the sufficient region. Neither a certified enclosure for all its displayed digits nor a description of the critical zeros is required.

Lemma 15 (Local positivity under a parameter decrease).

Let (a,c)∈Ω(a,c)\in\Omega and suppose ma,c≥0m_{a,c}\geq 0 on [0,∞)[0,\infty). For all sufficiently small h>0h>0,

First make the positivity near the origin uniform in the parameters. Choose a compact parameter neighborhood N⊂ΩN\subset\Omega containing all sufficiently small perturbations under consideration; when c=0c=0, take NN one-sided in the cc-variable. By (6.2),

μ0:=min(r,d)∈N⁡(r2+d)>0.\mu_{0}:=\min_{(r,d)\in N}\left(\dfrac{r}{2}+d\right)>0.

mr,d​(t)≥μ02>0,(r,d)∈N,0≤t≤ε.m_{r,d}(t)\geq\dfrac{\mu_{0}}{2}>0,\qquad(r,d)\in N,\quad 0\leq t\leq\varepsilon.

At the other end, the tail estimates of Lemma 5 are positive uniformly in the same parameter neighborhoods. For changes of aa with c=0c=0, use the fixed-cc estimate. For changes of c>0c>0, choose NN entirely inside 0<c<10<c<1, where the joint estimate applies. Increasing TT if necessary, these observations reduce every remaining sign question to the fixed compact interval [ε,T]⊂(0,∞)[\varepsilon,T]\subset(0,\infty).

The zeros of the original density in that interval are finite in number, because the density is entire and is not identically zero. If there are no zeros, compactness and continuity prove the stated stability. Otherwise, choose small neighborhoods of all zeros. Lemma 14 and continuity of the parameter derivatives show that, on these neighborhoods and for parameters sufficiently close to the original ones, the relevant parameter derivative is at most −γ-\gamma for some γ>0\gamma>0. For instance,

ma−h,c​(t)=ma,c​(t)−∫a−ha∂rmr,c​(t)​𝑑r≥ma,c​(t)+γ​h>0.m_{a-h,c}(t)=m_{a,c}(t)-\int_{a-h}^{a}\partial_{r}m_{r,c}(t)\,\mathrm{d}r\geq m_{a,c}(t)+\gamma h>0.

The same argument applies to a decrease of cc. On the compact complement of the zero neighborhoods, the original density has a positive minimum, which persists by continuity. Combining these estimates with the origin and tail estimates proves the lemma. ∎

Proposition 16 (Coordinatewise decrease of parameters).

If a>0a>0, 0≤c<10\leq c<1 and Ha,c∈BFH_{a,c}\in\mathrm{BF}, then

(6.13) Ha′,c′∈BFwhenever0<a′≤a,0≤c′≤c.H_{a^{\prime},c^{\prime}}\in\mathrm{BF}\qquad\text{whenever}\qquad 0<a^{\prime}\leq a,\quad 0\leq c^{\prime}\leq c.

The set of admissible parameters is relatively closed in (0,∞)×[0,1)(0,\infty)\times[0,1): for each fixed y>0y>0 and each derivative order, the derivatives of Ha,c​(y)H_{a,c}(y) depend continuously on (a,c)(a,c), and all Bernstein sign inequalities pass to the limit. Every admissible pair satisfies a+c<K0<3a+c<K_{0}<3, so decreasing a coordinate stays inside the representation domain.

Fix one coordinate and vary the other. Suppose a larger value qq is admissible but a smaller positive value pp is not. The closed nonempty set of admissible values in [p,q][p,q] has a minimum r>pr>p. Lemma 15 gives admissible values immediately to the left of rr, contradicting its minimality. For the cc-coordinate this argument first applies to 0<p<q0<p<q; passage to p=0p=0 is justified by relative closedness. This proves (6.13) by decreasing the two coordinates successively.

For strict positivity, suppose a coordinate has been strictly decreased and the resulting admissible density has a zero. By Lemma 14, a sufficiently small increase of that coordinate makes the density negative at the zero. But the increased parameter still lies below the original admissible coordinate, so (6.13) says that it must remain admissible. This is a contradiction. The argument also applies at c′=0c^{\prime}=0, using the right derivative there; no tail estimate uniform across c=0c=0 is needed. ∎

The content of Proposition 16 is specific to this family. It is not an inference that arbitrary products, quotients or parameter changes preserve the Bernstein class. In the original variables, increasing bb towards zero corresponds to decreasing cc.

7. The optimal boundary

We now distinguish an optimal boundary from the explicit sufficient line. The interval property is proved first, rather than assumed in the definition of a supremum.

Theorem 17 (The exact boundary as a monotone graph).

There is a unique continuous, strictly increasing function

A:(−1,0]⟶(0,α∗]A:(-1,0]\longrightarrow(0,\alpha_{*}]

Contact with zero and strict positivity below the boundary. Proposition 16 gives strict positivity when a<T⁡(c)a<T(c). 7.1. A necessary and sufficient zero-contact criterion

Corollary 18 (Global positivity and contact characterize the boundary).

Let a>0a>0, −1<b≤0-1<b\leq 0 and a−b<3a-b<3. Then a=A⁡(b)a=A(b) if and only if

(7.5) Da,−b​(t)≥0for all ​t≥0,Da,−b​(tb)=0for some ​tb>0.D_{a,-b}(t)\geq 0\quad\text{for all }t\geq 0,\qquad D_{a,-b}(t_{b})=0\quad\text{for some }t_{b}>0.

Every such zero has finite even order at least two; in particular,

(7.6) ∂tDa,−b​(tb)=0,∂t2Da,−b​(tb)≥0.\partial_{t}D_{a,-b}(t_{b})=0,\qquad\partial_{t}^{2}D_{a,-b}(t_{b})\geq 0.

At a contact point, the parameter derivatives satisfy

(7.7) ∂aDa,c​(tb)<0,∂cDa,c​(tb)<0,c=−b.\partial_{a}D_{a,c}(t_{b})<0,\qquad\partial_{c}D_{a,c}(t_{b})<0,\qquad c=-b.
Proof.

The forward implication follows from Theorem 17. Conversely, global nonnegativity in (7.5) gives a≤A⁡(b)a\leq A(b) by the Bernstein criterion. The existence of a zero excludes a<A⁡(b)a<A(b) by the strict-positivity assertion of that theorem. Thus a=A⁡(b)a=A(b). A zero of a nonnegative, nonzero real-analytic function at an interior point has finite even order. Finally, D=et​mD=e^{t}m, so Lemma 14 gives (7.7). ∎

Remark 19 (Scope of the implicit characterization).

The system Da,−b​(t)=∂tDa,−b​(t)=0D_{a,-b}(t)=\partial_{t}D_{a,-b}(t)=0 provides candidate contact points, but it is not sufficient on its own. The global inequality Da,−b≥0D_{a,-b}\geq 0 in (7.5) is essential. A tangency can occur while the density is negative elsewhere. The theorem does not assert uniqueness of the contact point, exact multiplicity two, or differentiability of AA. Thus (7.1) and (7.5) are an exact implicit description, not an elementary closed formula or a certified numerical evaluation of the boundary.

The zero-contact criterion also gives a direct numerical formulation of the optimal boundary. For fixed −1<b<0-1<b<0, define

A floating-point implementation of the bisection procedure is only a numerical approximation and is not by itself a proof of the sign of MM. The quantitative form of Lemma 5, especially (3.23), gives a parameter-uniform remainder estimate on every compact parameter box KK contained in the interior domain. If LKL_{K} denotes the positive minimum of the leading coefficient and CKC_{K} is any verified upper bound for the constant in (3.23), then any concrete T≥TKT\geq T_{K} satisfying

7.3. Tangency equations and conditional continuation

At a boundary point, every contact satisfies

(7.15) Da,c​(t)=0,∂tDa,c​(t)=0,a=A⁡(−c),0<c<1.D_{a,c}(t)=0,\qquad\partial_{t}D_{a,c}(t)=0,\qquad a=A(-c),\quad 0<c<1.

Consequently, solving the two equations in (7.15) for (a,t)(a,t) at fixed cc is a useful fast predictor for the boundary. As emphasized in Remark 19, however, the system alone is not a certificate: after a candidate (a,t)(a,t) is found one must still verify

Da,c​(s)≥0for every ​s≥0.D_{a,c}(s)\geq 0\qquad\text{for every }s\geq 0.

The bracketed procedure above provides such a global check and can therefore be combined with Newton or quasi-Newton iterations for speed.

The present results do not prove that the boundary contact is unique or always of exact order two. The next local continuation statement therefore assumes both uniqueness and nondegeneracy; these hypotheses prevent a competing contact branch from becoming the active global boundary.

8. Bounds and examples

8.1. Necessary bounds, a sufficient line, and an exact implicit graph

For −1<b≤0-1<b\leq 0, the admissible set is

𝒜b={a>0:Fa,b∈BF}=(0,A⁡(b)].\mathcal{A}_{b}=\{a>0:F_{a,b}\in\mathrm{BF}\}=(0,A(b)].

The roles of the three descriptions are different. The inequalities a<U⁡(b)a<U(b) are explicit necessary tests. The inequality a≤α∗​(1+b)a\leq\alpha_{*}(1+b) is an explicit sufficient condition in terms of the exact one-parameter constant. The condition a≤A⁡(b)a\leq A(b) is necessary and sufficient, with AA determined implicitly by Corollary 18. Thus, for −1<b<0-1<b<0,

(8.1) (0,α∗​(1+b)]⊊(0,A⁡(b)]⊂(0,min⁡{α∗,U⁡(b)}).(0,\alpha_{*}(1+b)]\subsetneq(0,A(b)]\subset(0,\min\{\alpha_{*},U(b)\}).

To locate the exact endpoint implicitly, one must impose global nonnegativity of D1,−bD_{1,-b} and contact with zero at a positive argument.

8.4. Scope of the boundary description

The no-gap theorem and strict coordinatewise ordering are the additional ingredients that turn a supremum into a genuine optimal boundary. The exact Bernstein region can be described either by a≤A⁡(b)a\leq A(b) or by β⁡(a)≤b≤0\beta(a)\leq b\leq 0. The contact criterion is valid without assuming that the zero is unique or nondegenerate. Solving only two tangency equations, or checking finitely many sample values of a density, does not certify global nonnegativity. An elementary formula for AA, a certified numerical evaluation for general negative bb, and a universal uniqueness theorem for the contact points are not claimed.

9. The boundary-contact conjecture and further problems

Theorem 17 proves that for each −1<b<0-1<b<0 the boundary density

DA⁡(b),−b​(t)D_{A(b),-b}(t)

is nonnegative on [0,∞)[0,\infty) and has a nonempty finite set of positive zeros. Corollary 18 shows that every such zero has finite even order at least two. What is not yet determined is whether more than one contact can occur or whether a boundary zero can have order four or higher. The numerical formulation in Subsection 7.2 and the local continuation result in Proposition 21 suggest the following sharper picture.

Conjecture 23 (Boundary-contact uniqueness).

For every −1<b<0-1<b<0 there exists a unique tb>0t_{b}>0 such that

(9.1) DA⁡(b),−b​(tb)=0.D_{A(b),-b}(t_{b})=0.

Moreover, this zero is exactly of order two; equivalently,

(9.2) Dt​(A⁡(b),−b,tb)=0,Dt​t​(A⁡(b),−b,tb)>0.D_{t}(A(b),-b,t_{b})=0,\qquad D_{tt}(A(b),-b,t_{b})>0.

The conjecture is deliberately separated from the proved characterization. Theorem 17 and Corollary 18 require neither uniqueness nor nondegeneracy, so none of the unconditional results of the paper depend on Conjecture 23.

If Conjecture 23 holds, its uniqueness and quadratic-contact assertions supply precisely the hypotheses of Proposition 21 at every interior boundary point. Consequently AA and b↦tbb\mapsto t_{b} are real analytic on (−1,0)(-1,0) and satisfy

(9.3) A′​(b)=DcDa|(a,c,t)=(A⁡(b),−b,tb)>0,A^{\prime}(b)=\dfrac{D_{c}}{D_{a}}\bigg|_{(a,c,t)=(A(b),-b,t_{b})}>0,

and

(9.4) tb′​(b)=Dt​c−Dt​a​A′​(b)Dt​t|(a,c,t)=(A⁡(b),−b,tb).t_{b}^{\prime}(b)=\dfrac{D_{tc}-D_{ta}A^{\prime}(b)}{D_{tt}}\bigg|_{(a,c,t)=(A(b),-b,t_{b})}.

Thus the conjecture would convert the presently implicit continuous boundary into a single analytic critical branch governed by the two tangency equations together with the global positivity condition.

Several related questions remain natural.

  1. (1)

    Prove or disprove Conjecture 23 analytically, without relying on a finite numerical sampling of the density.

  2. (2)

    Determine the endpoint asymptotics of A⁡(b)A(b) and tbt_{b} as b↑0b\uparrow 0 and as b↓−1b\downarrow-1. In particular, it would be useful to identify the first nontrivial correction to the sufficient line α∗​(1+b)\alpha_{*}(1+b) near either endpoint.

  3. (3)

    Develop certified high-precision enclosures of A⁡(b)A(b) on a mesh of bb-values by combining the variational formula (7.9), the uniform tail bounds of Lemma 5, and interval arithmetic. Such data could test the uniqueness conjecture and suggest asymptotic formulas, but would remain logically separate from a proof.

  4. (4)

    Determine whether the derivative formula (9.3) admits effective upper and lower bounds depending only on bb, and whether these lead to sharper explicit two-sided estimates for A⁡(b)A(b) than those in Theorem 17.

The central open issue is therefore no longer the existence of an optimal boundary, which has been established above, but the fine geometry of its critical contact with the Laplace density. A proof of Conjecture 23 would provide a natural next step from the exact implicit solution toward a differential and computationally explicit description of the Alzer–Berg boundary.
